candidates.abstract: Abstract Humans are able to track the change of color and orientation (CO) of an object at a stunning rate. We show that (1) binding requires a rapid recurrent modulation (~120 ms) of activity in V1/V2, whose latency is independent of the alternation rate. (2) Performance drops to chance when the alternation rate becomes too high to accommodate the recurrent process within a single alternation. candidates.abstract: Abstract Compact control of optical orbital angular momentum (OAM) is central to chip-scale photonic integration. The paradigm transition from lens-type to cavity-type vortices provides an ultra-compact OAM platform, advancing chip-scale integration.

candidates.abstract: Abstract From molecular assemblies to multicellular tissues, chirality organizes living and active-matter systems into striking collective states. Finally, we show that the dynamics of these instabilities play an important role, with slow polar reorientations shifting the dielectric response to very low frequencies and overdamped tilting modes producing persistent Raman central peaks. candidates.abstract: Acoustic waves transport mechanical energy and elastic strain through solids, with material composition and shape governing their propagation. In the gigahertz hypersound regime, acoustic wavelengths reach tens to hundreds of nanometres, comparable to nanoscale device dimensions. Harnessing these waves underpins high-frequency signal processing, sensing, electromagnetic coupling and quantum control. Acoustic metrology probes elastic modes and internal interfaces. Yet directly imaging how nanoscale acoustic waves interact with local structure remains challenging, requiring picometre displacement sensitivity combined with high spatiotemporal resolution. Here we demonstrate full-field imaging of laser-induced hypersound at surfaces using reflected electron wavefronts. We introduce ultrafast low-energy electron microscopy (ULEEM), exploiting the intrinsic surface sensitivity of few-electronvolt electrons. Coherent electron pulses down to femtosecond durations reflect from the topmost atomic layers, imprinting the evolving surface profile onto their wavefronts. Defocus converts phase variations into image contrast. In a thin van der Waals material, we image the thermoelastic generation and propagation of picometre-amplitude acoustic waves. Measured dispersion relations, interpreted through elastodynamic modelling, distinguish substrate-supported and locally detached regions, revealing how interfacial contact shapes propagation. Delayed wave emission reveals scattering at buried mechanical defects. Our results establish electron-wavefront imaging of nanoscale surface dynamics, enabling the exploration of ultrafast energy transport, structural transformations and coupled mechanical, electronic and magnetic phenomena.

Recently, interest has grown in translating on-surface synthetic protocols from noble metal surfaces to insulating surfaces, which offer technological relevance, and to magnetic or superconducting surfaces, which offer new routes to correlated phases. It is important, therefore, to understand how these alternative surfaces may alter the properties of adsorbates through processes like charge transfer and screening. Evidence for charge transfer is often obtained experimentally via scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS), and theoretically via density functional theory (DFT). Consistent with these predictions, longer carboxylate chains suppress H$_2$S evolution more effectively. Because thicker coatings also hinder Li-ion transport, intermediate chain lengths offer the best balance between moisture protection and ionic conductivity.

candidates.abstract: The Hubbard model offers a powerful minimal description of strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials, yet it neglects effects observed in nature that give rise to a much richer variety of physics. For instance, including nonlocal interactions introduces a competition between strongly correlated phases, while incorporating spin-orbit coupling (SOC) can lead to the emergence of exotic topological phases. Seeking a more realistic platform for simulating graphene and, potentially, related materials such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), we therefore consider the extended Kane-Mele-Hubbard model, which features a Kane-Mele SOC term and nearest-neighbor interactions. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $α=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. candidates.abstract: Predicting the properties of correlated materials and molecules often requires a many-body description that goes beyond single-particle and mean-field approximations. Tensor networks address this challenge by exploiting the entanglement structure of quantum states to construct compact, systematically improvable representations. This Perspective introduces their underlying principles and examines how network geometry, bond-dimension truncation, and approximate contraction determine the accuracy and computational reach of these approaches. We survey applications across regimes of increasing complexity, ranging from ground-state properties of quantum magnets and itinerant-fermion systems to excitation spectra, nonequilibrium dynamics, finite-temperature and open systems, and molecular electronic structure. Throughout, we evaluate the maturity of existing capabilities and their principal limitations, synthesizing this assessment into a practical method-selection guide. We argue that reliable materials predictions require quantifying uncertainties introduced at each stage, from constructing material-specific Hamiltonians to extracting experimentally accessible observables. Finally, we identify the algorithmic advances and reproducible computational practices needed to establish tensor networks as a routine tool for predictive materials science and quantum chemistry.

candidates.abstract: Conventional particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) has been the standard diagnostic tool for studying fluid and granular flows. However, in dense granular systems, the average distance moved by particles between frames can approach or exceed inter-particle spacing, demanding ultra-high frame rates. Furthermore, neighbouring particles may move together, and common velocity-based prediction fails after energetic collisions. Existing methods struggle to track granular particles without losing identities or swapping. We present Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry (CBTV), a training-free multi-pass method leveraging multicoloured particles to achieve enhanced tracking. CBTV first matches constellations of neighbouring coloured particles as single units, guided by a cross-correlation motion prior, and only then assigns the remaining particles individually. We compare it with 12 baseline tracker configurations, from classical linkers to graph-neural-network and transformer models, on 59 cases from 15 simulated discrete-element granular flows with exact ground truth (0.006-9 diameters/frame). CBTV matches or exceeds every tracker tested on an impulsive collision at every displacement. Its advantage lies in dense flows in which particles move between about half and twice their spacing per frame, where links between frames are ambiguous. On agitated shear flow, a colour relaxation tracker, which also uses neighbour context, matches or narrowly exceeds CBTV. Where links are unambiguous, CBTV is close to the best tracker, and beyond about two to three particle diameters per frame, the range of its motion prior, trackers that compensate for bulk motion are more accurate. For experimentalists, dense granular flows of coloured particles can be tracked at displacements per frame where trackers without neighbour context lose identities, easing the demand for ultra-high frame rates without training data.

candidates.abstract: Hierarchical and modular organization defines brain architecture, yet how it supports flexible computation and functional specialization remains unclear. Although dynamic range is a hallmark of efficient information processing, its distribution across modules and hierarchical levels remains largely unexplored. Here, we show that hierarchical-modular networks naturally generate heterogeneous modular dynamics and firing rates, extending regimes of critical-like dynamics with enhanced intrinsic timescales, reflecting critical slowing down, and diverse scaling exponents without fine-tuning near criticality. Intrinsic timescales increase across hierarchical levels, while their dispersion within levels emerges only when connectivity profiles and firing rates are heterogeneous. We introduce modular dynamic range to quantify how individual modules respond to external inputs and show that heterogeneity enhances both global and module-specific sensitivity, with modular intrinsic timescales increasing with dynamic range. Local stimulation reduces dynamic range in homogeneous networks but enhances it in heterogeneous networks relative to global stimulation. Moreover, selectively stimulating intermediate hierarchical levels maximizes both global and modular dynamic range, revealing a principle of functional specialization. In heterogeneous networks, modular dynamic range is more variable and increases even in unstimulated modules, demonstrating distributed computational benefits beyond directly stimulated regions. Together, these findings establish heterogeneity as a mechanism through which hierarchical-modular networks sustain critical-like dynamics, generate hierarchical timescales, and distribute computational sensitivity, providing a basis for functional specialization without fine-tuning to criticality.

candidates.abstract: During joint training, backpropagation allows later layers to reshape earlier representations, a feedback mechanism absent from purely layer-wise learning. We extend Neural Low-Degree Filtering (Neural LoFi), a recently proposed layer-wise spectral surrogate for feature learning, to capture this interaction. Starting from the exact backpropagation gradients, we derive a local coupling between a neuron's incoming weights and its corresponding next-layer column. In a controlled small-initialization regime with smooth activations and fixed surroundings, these dynamics amplify singular modes of a cross-layer correlation operator. Each growing mode pairs an earlier feature with an upper-layer response through shared neuron coefficients. This motivates a backward-coupling algorithm in which upper-layer sensitivities generate sample-dependent effective labels for earlier spectral steps, while corrected features refine upward transmission. A function-space variational principle characterizes the selected feature-response pairs by maximizing the label correlation of their product under kernel-norm constraints. For three-layer networks, we derive self-consistent continuous-time dynamics for the filtered hidden-layer features, the activation kernels, and the network output under the proposed backward coupling. In a hierarchical multi-index model, we establish a feature-recovery separation: backward coupling recovers lower-layer directions invisible to the original forward label-weighted statistic. The linear specialization recovers residual-dependent singular-mode dynamics, while paired modes provide a dynamical mechanism for linked low-rank covariance components consistent with the rainbow-network picture. Experiments with fully connected and convolutional networks on binary CIFAR-10 show improved accuracy over forward Neural LoFi at matched widths.
